what-changes-when-you-bring-your-own-nod.text: The diagram shows the same runner reaching two different chains. On the left, the factory default: the runner spawns a private cardano node, funds itself from a genesis key carried in the archive, and talks to it on network magic forty-two. On the right, external mode: the same runner connects to the preprod node you already run, funds itself from your own signing key file, and talks to it on network magic one.

External mode is not a second implementation. It hands the shared entry point a socket path, a network magic and a signing key file instead of letting it spawn a devnet. Everything downstream — the transaction builders, the validators, the proofs, the read-backs — is the code the factory devnet exercises on every run.

The table lists the three things you supply: the node's node-to-client socket, the network magic, and the wallet signing key file. Each has a command-line flag and an environment variable, and flags win over environment variables.

Give none of the three and you get the factory devnet, exactly as before. Give one or two and the runner refuses, naming the one it is missing, because a half-configured run would otherwise submit devnet transactions to a public network.

step-1-download-the-release-and-check-it.text: Take the archive and its checksum manifest from the release page, extract it, then check the bytes with sha two five six sum and the compiled validator identities with the archive's own verify script.

The verify script re-derives every validator hash from the compiled blueprints the archive carries and compares them with the pinned manifest. It needs only bash and jq. If it exits non-zero, stop: the archive does not carry the validators the release claims, and nothing below is meaningful.

step-2-point-at-your-preprod-node.text: You need a cardano node synced to preprod and its node-to-client socket path — the one the node's own configuration names.

Two facts the runners check for you. First, the network magic must be the one the node runs; preprod is one. The handshake negotiates it, a node on another network refuses the connection, and the runner turns that refusal into a message naming the socket and the magic you asked for.

Second, protocol parameters come from the node. Fees, execution unit prices and size limits are queried from the running node on every session, never taken from a devnet constant, so a preprod parameter change is picked up on the next run with no code change.
Mainnet's magic is refused outright. These runners submit live transactions to demonstrate a lifecycle; they are for test networks.

step-3-create-and-fund-a-wallet.text: The wallet is yours. Its key is read from a file on your machine, used to sign, and never printed, logged or transmitted anywhere but into a transaction witness.
The commands shown generate a payment key pair with cardano cli and build the matching testnet address.

The runners accept the cardano cli signing key file as written — the JSON text envelope with its cborHex field. The same key as bare hex, or as thirty-two raw bytes, works too. The address the runner uses is derived from the key in that file, so the address you fund and the address that pays cannot disagree.

Fund the address from the preprod faucet, then send one self-payment of a few ada back to the same address. The faucet pays a single output; the second payment leaves the wallet holding a small ada-only output, which is what a Plutus transaction spends as collateral.

step-4-run-a-journey.text: Start with the canonical initialization runner, the shortest run that touches the chain, passing the socket, the magic and the key file.
The naming journey the demo is about is three more runners in order: register rows, recovery rows, retirement rows.

Together they claim a name, fold it with its real representative, rotate its control through the committed next controller, retire it into completion-only custody, and complete the retirement permissionlessly so the name reads Over and can never be claimed again.

what-a-run-looks-like.text: Each runner narrates what it did and what it then observed on chain. The first line names the chain and the wallet: the mode, the socket, the magic and the funding address.

Then one line per step, each stating the observation rather than the intent — the transaction identifier, the datum read back, the hash that matched. A zero exit is the claim: every runner exits non-zero on any mismatch, and it checks by reading state back from the node, never by assuming its own submission worked.

The sequence diagram shows one run. You supply the socket, magic and key file. The runner performs the node-to-client handshake at that magic, which the node refuses if it is another network. It queries protocol parameters, queries the funding address, and refuses immediately if the wallet cannot pay. Then, for each step of the journey, it submits a transaction, polls until the output that transaction created is visible, and asserts what it read back. It ends with exit zero, or a named mismatch.

waiting-for-confirmations.text: A public test network makes a block about every twenty seconds; the factory devnet makes one about every second. The runners do not assume either.

After a submission they poll the node for an output the transaction actually created and continue the moment it appears, giving up after five minutes with a message naming the transaction that never landed.
So a preprod run is slower than a devnet run — minutes rather than seconds per journey — and it is slow in proportion to the network, not to a constant someone guessed.

when-the-wallet-cannot-pay.text: The funding check runs before the first transaction is built, so a wallet problem is a message and not a balance exception in the middle of a lifecycle.

The message shown names the address to fund, the lovelace held and across how many outputs, the lovelace required, the largest ada-only output and the collateral required, and then the faucet link and the self-payment step that fixes it.
The two numbers are a floor rather than a promise: they catch the empty and the nearly-empty wallet at the start of a run, and a journey that runs long can still exhaust a thinly funded wallet later.

other-refusals-you-may-see.text: A table of five refusals and what each means.
A refused node-to-client connection for a network magic means the node runs a different network, or the socket path is not a node-to-client socket.
Partially configured external mode means one or two of the three settings were given; all three are required together.
A refused magic seven six four eight two four zero seven three is mainnet; these runners are for test networks.
A wallet key file that does not hold thirty-two key bytes is not a payment signing key — a verification key or a stake key produces this.
And a transaction accepted by the node but never carried by a block within five minutes means the node may not be synced, or the network is not producing blocks.

running-it-again.text: Reruns are safe and expected. Each run claims its own fresh name and boots its own registry from a seed it designates out of your wallet's own outputs, so a second run does not collide with the first and does not depend on it having finished.

Nothing in the archive holds state between runs; what persists lives on chain, under identities each run derives and prints. If a run fails part way, rerun it — the failed run's on-chain leftovers are inert, because they belong to that run's own registry token and no later run reads them.

what-this-page-does-not-cover.text: The canonical deployment on preprod — a published registry identity with its seed reference, applied script hashes, policy identifiers and bootstrap transactions — is recorded separately once it exists, from real values. Nothing here publishes or claims a canonical identity; each run stands up its own.

run-the-folder.text: As a folder, you can let the node determine how many requests fit in each transaction. The registry journey uses fold all on a private devnet. Each attempt reports its batch size and outcome. Refused batches are halved; confirmed batches update the mirror before fresh proofs are computed against the chain root. A request refused alone is reported and skipped for the rest of the invocation, and stays on chain. A stale proof mirror stops the run. The folder runbook describes the library interface and the real node test that drains multiple batches.
